lines: Two real failures are injected together into a small replicated register: a delayed acknowledgement, and a duplicated message.
A read happens after both. Does the resulting recorded history, checked mechanically, turn out consistent with any honest real-time order at all?
answer: The checker finds a real violation.

lines: Run it for real: the checker scans the real recorded history and finds it genuinely is not linearizable.
Every real total order gets checked, mechanically, by genuine enumeration rather than by assumption.
Of the two real failures injected together, only one actually shows up as a violation in the recorded history.
Does the checker name the delayed-acknowledgement read, or the duplicated-message read, as the real problem?
Run it for real: the checker names the delayed-acknowledgement read directly, the duplicated-message read caused no actual violation at all, because it was idempotent.
steps.takeaway: Not every injected failure leaves a trace; only the one an actual read observes ever shows up in a history.

lines: Now the identical two failures run again, except the lagging replica catches up before anyone reads from it.
Is the resulting history now linearizable?
answer: The duplicated message was never the problem.

lines: Run it for real: genuinely linearizable now, even with that same duplicated-message failure still injected.
steps.takeaway: A failure a real read never observes can be injected all day without ever showing up as a violation.

lines: Now a read genuinely overlaps a write in real time: neither one finishes before the other starts.
How many of the real total orders the checker brute force enumerates actually respect that real-time precedence?
answer: Either order genuinely respects real-time precedence.

lines: Run it for real: exactly two, matching the real order structure of a single concurrent pair, found by the checker's own brute force enumeration, not assumed.
steps.takeaway: A genuinely concurrent pair's own real order count comes from its real structure, never a hand-picked guess.

lines: One real, widely used testing methodology states this exact structure directly, in its own words.
A generator makes operations, a history records them, a nemesis injects real faults, and a checker decides correctness.
So here's the shape of this whole topic: a recorded history gathered under several real, independent failures can be mechanically checked for linearizability.
Only the failures an actual read observes ever show up as a violation; the rest can be injected all day and leave no trace at all.
A real checker finds the answer by genuine enumeration over every candidate order, never by assumption.
